Authors: Sapakova, S., Sapakov, A., Auyelbekov, O., Tukenova, L., Tynymbayev, S., Ualiyev, Z., Skakova, A., & Kabdoldina, A.
Exact article title: A Web-Based Digital Twin for Traffic and Air Quality Monitoring: A Prototype Study in Almaty, Kazakhstan
Study objective: Prototype platform integrating traffic, air-quality monitoring, exposure indexing and short-horizon PM2.5 prediction
Data source: OpenWeather Air Pollution API (primary), WAQI (secondary), OpenWeather Current Weather API, TomTom Traffic Flow API
Dataset size: 18,330 raw records; 4,961 real co-located observations; 1,222 samples at 15 min
Temporal resolution: ~5 min raw; modelled at 15 min (also 30 and 60 min)
Target variable: PM2.5 at the next time step (t+1)
Forecast horizon: One step ahead (15 min primary; 30 and 60 min sensitivity)
Preprocessing methods: Removal of fallback records, range checks, aggregation to fixed intervals, chronological sorting
Feature engineering: PM2.5 and traffic lags (1,2,3,6,12 steps); 3- and 6-step rolling means; hour, day of week, weekend
Models used: Lag-1 persistence, Linear Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting
MAE: Reported in Table 7 (values not legible in accessible text)
R²: Persistence 0.980 at 15 min (ML 0.962–0.977); at 60 min persistence 0.743, ML ≤ 0.319
Other reported performance metrics: RF importance: current PM2.5 ≈0.72, 3-step rolling mean ≈0.24
Strongest reported result and its evalua: Persistence R² = 0.980 for 15-min nowcasting on a summer test segment
Strengths: Uses the same OpenWeather Air Pollution API in Kazakhstan; chronological evaluation; explicit persistence baseline
Limitations: Only 18 active summer days (outside heating season); very short horizon; small samples at coarser resolution
Relevance to our project: Closest data-source match (OpenWeather API, Kazakhstan); shows that persistence is hard to beat at short horizons
Why the paper was selected: Only identified peer-reviewed study using OpenWeather pollution data with ML in Kazakhstan
How we will apply its methods: Adopt persistence benchmark, chronological split, lag/rolling features; extend to a day-ahead horizon and multi-year history
Directly comparable with ours?: No — 15-min nowcasting vs our day-ahead daily mean
Verification status: Verified: metadata, design and R² values from publisher page; MAE/RMSE not legible

Authors: Agibayeva, A., Khalikhan, R., Guney, M., Karaca, F., Torezhan, A., & Avcu, E.
Exact article title: An Air Quality Modeling and Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALY) Risk Assessment Case Study: Comparing Statistical and Machine Learning Approaches for PM2.5 Forecasting
Study objective: Compare MLR and RF for PM2.5 and estimate health burden (DALY)
Data source: Kazhydromet National Air Quality Monitoring Network; Bureau of National Statistics

Limitations: Concurrent predictors (not a forecast); single year; two stations; random split

Why the paper was selected: Only verified ML PM2.5 study for Astana
How we will apply its methods: Heating-season definition in EDA/E7; include PM10 and CO history as predictors (lagged, not concurrent)

Supporting section/table: Section 2.4 (split/CV); Section 3.4 + Table 5 (MLR); Section 3.5 + Table 6 (RF); Section 3.7, Tables 8 & 10 (DALY)

Authors: Fetahi, E., Ovuoraye, P., Canhasi, E., Susuri, A., & Misini, A.
Exact article title: Multi-horizon air pollution prediction using interpretable machine learning techniques in a growing urban area
Study objective: Compare ML models for PM2.5 at several horizons with SHAP interpretation
Forecast horizon: 1 h and 24 h (others not stated in abstract)
Feature engineering: Pollutant lags, rolling statistics, cyclical time encoding

Authors: Psomadakis, I., Christakis, C., Metallidou, C. L., Panagiotakopoulos, T., Katsafadou, A. I., & Kiouvrekis, Y.
Exact article title: Forecasting of PM2.5/PM10 Using Machine Learning: A Benchmarking Study Based on Open Air Quality IoT Datasets
Study objective: Benchmark ML models for next-day and 7-day-maximum PM forecasting
Data source: Hellenic Ministry of Environment and Energy
Preprocessing methods: Chronological 70/15/15 boundaries fixed first; interpolation of gaps ≤5 days within partitions; standardization fit on training
Feature engineering: Univariate past-only: lags 1–28 days, trailing 3/7/14-day means and SDs, sin/cos day-of-year/day-of-week, weekend
Models used: RF, SVM (RBF), feed-forward NN, LSTM; persistence and SARIMA baselines
Training procedure: 40 sliding windows (50% train / 10% validation) in first 80%
Other reported performance metrics: SARIMA underperformed persistence at several stations
Strengths: Strict past-only features, persistence baseline, chronological assessment
Limitations: R² only; test-period variance shift; SARIMA not refit
Relevance to our project: Same target type (next-day daily PM2.5) and same feature families
How we will apply its methods: Fix chronological boundaries before any processing; univariate lag/rolling design; SVR as a candidate
Directly comparable with ours?: Partly — same horizon/target but station data and R²-only reporting
Supporting section/table: Abstract & Section 8 (13/20 wins); Section 6.1, Table 8, Figure 9 (next-day R2); Section 6.3 (Volos-1 R2 0.458); Sections 4.2, 4.4, 4.4.1 (design, persistence)
Verification status: Verified metadata and design; numeric tables not legible

Authors: Chivukula, S., Cortes Santos, A. J., Delgado, R., Arachchige, D. K., Caraballo-Vega, J. A., & Friberg, M. D.
Exact article title: An Applied Assessment of Multi-Source Data Fusion by Machine Learning for PM2.5 Daily Concentration Prediction
Study objective: Assess fusion of regulatory, low-cost and satellite PM2.5 for next-day prediction
Dataset name: EPA AQS, PurpleAir, ACAG satellite PM2.5
Preprocessing methods: Completeness rules (≥75% hourly data), sensor QC, interpolation, RobustScaler fit on training
Feature engineering: 1-day lag, 7-day rolling mean and SD, sin/cos day-of-year, source indicators
Models used: LSTM; persistence, linear regression, RF, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost baselines
Strongest reported result and its evalua: XGBoost R² 0.667 on a 2023 temporal hold-out
Strengths: Year-based train/validation/test design like ours; persistence baseline; tree models beat LSTM
Limitations: Interpolation over full record (possible leakage); seed not fixed; city results not comparable
Relevance to our project: Same split philosophy (train years / validation year / test year) and day-ahead target
Why the paper was selected: Seed paper; recent daily next-day benchmark with boosting
How we will apply its methods: Year-based chronological split; completeness threshold for daily means; XGBoost and RF candidates
Directly comparable with ours?: Partly — day-ahead daily target, but different data and R²-focused
Supporting section/table: Section 3.6 Baseline Model Comparisons, Table 6; Table 4 (split years)

Exact article title: Benchmark-Driven Model Selection for Forecasting over Open Gridded Urban Air-Quality Fields

Dataset name: Open-Meteo Air Quality (CAMS Europe) + Open-Meteo historical weather

Feature engineering: Lags t-1…t-28; rolling mean/SD/max over 3–28 days ending t-1; calendar; issue-day meteorology

Authors: Makhdoomi, A., Sarkhosh, M., & Ziaei, S.
Exact article title: PM2.5 concentration prediction using machine learning algorithms: an approach to virtual monitoring stations
Study objective: Estimate PM2.5 for virtual stations from meteorology
Dataset name: LDAPS + IMO meteorology; AQM PM data
Preprocessing methods: Listwise deletion; IQR outlier removal; Spearman screening (|ρ|>0.1)
Feature engineering: Visibility, wind, rain, humidity, dust reports (+AQI/PM10 apparently)
Strongest reported result and its evalua: GBR R² 0.9802 on a random 20% test
Limitations: Concurrent AQI/PM10 inputs inflate skill; random split; no baseline; outliers removed
Relevance to our project: Cautionary example: very high R² from concurrent estimation is not comparable with forecasting
Why the paper was selected: Seed paper; used to discuss leakage and comparability
How we will apply its methods: Keep extremes; forbid concurrent pollutant inputs; persistence baseline
